"You look for the assumption that makes a problem slow, or makes extra compute buy only more of the same. Ask which part
of the work waits on another part, and whether it must. Ask which quantity is measured, and whether a different but
related quantity would be cheaper to compute, easier to split, or more informative. Ask whether the unit of work is the
right one, or whether the work could be cut, merged or reordered. Ask whether the objective is the right one: the single
best answer, a ranking, a distribution, a rare tail, or a yes or no. Ask what is held fixed that need not be. Prefer
changes that alter what more compute buys over changes that only run the same work more times.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me analyze this problem carefully.

The problem: Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, conceptors, etc.) to improve robot manipulation. Current work has shown steering works on rigid tabletop tasks (pick-and-place, drawers), but nobody knows if steering features exist for contact-rich or deformable tasks (cloth folding, dish loading). Compute currently buys: more SAEs fit + more closed-loop rollouts, each rollout sequential (300 steps × 150ms forward passes), and rollouts are independent so they could be batched — but sim batching only helps if steering effects transfer sim→real, which is false for cloth.

Key assumptions to attack:

1. **The assumption that the evaluation unit must be a full closed-loop rollout.** To find whether a feature controls contact-rich behavior, maybe you don't need 300-step rollouts. You could measure open-loop quantities: does steering feature X change the predicted action distribution on contact-rich frames? Measure per-step action divergence on a held-out dataset of cloth/dish interactions rather than full episodes. That changes what's measured from "task success over 300 sequential steps" to "action-distribution shift per observation," which is embarrassingly parallel across frames — you can batch thousands of frames through the VLA with hooks on one GPU. The sequential dependency (each step waits on the next observation) disappears if you use recorded observations instead of rolled-out ones. Risk: open-loop action shift may not predict closed-loop success (compounding errors, causal confusion). Cheapest measurement: take an existing cloth-manipulation dataset (e.g., from DROID there may be little cloth... there are cloth datasets like ClothFloods? or the RT-1/RT-X has some deformable tasks; there's "Folding" tasks in some datasets) — measure correlation between per-step action divergence under steering and ... hmm, you need ground truth of success. Actually the question: does open-loop steering-induced action divergence on contact-rich frames predict closed-loop success deltas? Measure: steer top-k features, compute KL or L2 between steered and unsteered action chunks on N recorded contact-rich observations; then run the much smaller set of closed-loop trials for the top few features and check rank correlation. Cost: a few GPU-days for the open-loop sweep vs months for closed loop. Closest prior: open-loop vs closed-loop evaluation gaps in VLAs are documented (e.g., OpenVLA folks note open-loop L2 doesn't predict closed-loop success).

2. **The assumption that the objective is "single best feature per task" measured by task success.** Reframe to: measure the distribution/coverage of behaviors a feature induces, or a yes/no screening question: "does ANY SAE feature exist whose clamping destroys or creates a contact-rich skill?" Instead of sweeping 520 SAEs × 135 features with 150 rollouts each on success, screen features with cheap proxy metrics (grasp-force stability, contact events in sim, cloth-coverage metric in sim) and only spend real-robot rollouts on the survivors. This changes the objective from estimating success rate precisely (150 rollouts to get ±few %) to a ranking/screening problem — best-arm identification / successive halving. Compute after: hyperband-style allocation means compute buys discrimination among top candidates rather than uniform precision. Question: what fraction of the 20,250 episodes were spent on features whose effect is distinguishable from zero within 10 rollouts? Measure: reanalyze existing rollout logs (zero compute — data already exists), apply sequential probability ratio test / successive halving retrospectively, count episodes saved. Cost: hours of an analyst's time, no GPU.

3. **The assumption that the sim-to-real gap for cloth is a fixed wall.** The text says batching sim rollouts "pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth)". Attack: is the sim-to-real gap for *steering effects* (the delta caused by a feature) the same as the gap for *policy behavior*? It's possible that absolute success rates don't transfer but relative steering-induced shifts do (the feature might encode something real because SAEs were fit on real data or on activations from real rollouts). So the reframe: measure the steering-effect correlation between sim and real on a small set of features; if the delta transfers even when absolute performance doesn't, then massive parallel sim screening becomes valid. Cheapest measurement: pick ~10 features with known real-robot effects on a rigid task (from the pi0.5/DROID experiments), replicate those steers in a sim of the same task, compute rank correlation of the steering delta; for cloth, do a tiny version with one deformable task. Cost: maybe 200-400 real rollouts (a few days on one DROID setup) + sim setup. Actually the rigid-task version needs no new real data — the published +9 to +21 out of 25 numbers exist; just need to reproduce in sim. Question: "Is the Spearman correlation between sim and real steering-induced success deltas across ≥10 features ≥ 0.7 on rigid tasks, and what is it on one cloth task?"

4. **What is held fixed that need not be:** the VLA forward pass at 150ms unbatched — could batch observation across environments (already covered by reframe 1/3). Also held fixed: the SAE is fit once and then features tested one at a time. Could instead do a search over the continuous steering direction space (e.g., optimize steering vector directly with a derivative-free method, CMA-ES) — that changes the unit of work from "enumerate dictionary features" to "optimize in activation space," where compute buys better search. But that's similar to conceptors. Maybe fold into another reframe.

5. **The assumption that evaluation needs task success at all.** Alternative: measure causal effect of features on internal prediction of contact-relevant quantities — e.g., train linear probes on tactile/force signals and measure whether steering changes predicted contact outcomes on recorded data. Again open-loop.

Let me pick the strongest three:

A. Change what's measured: from closed-loop success to open-loop action-divergence screening on recorded contact-rich observations. Kills the sequential rollout dependency, makes everything batchable. Key risk: open-loop doesn't predict closed-loop (documented concern). Cheap measure: rank correlation between open-loop divergence and closed-loop success deltas on the already-completed 135-feature rigid sweep — zero new rollouts needed if logs exist. Then extrapolate check on cloth.

Wait — the 135-feature sweep with 150 rollouts each: if the logs exist, you can compute both open-loop divergence (cheap, one GPU-day) and you already have closed-loop success, then measure correlation. That's the cheapest validation. Cost: ~1 GPU-week for recomputing steered forward passes on recorded frames (135 features × say 10k frames — that's 1.35M forward passes, at 150ms unbatched that's 56 GPU-hours, batched much less).

Question: "On the existing 135-feature sweep, what is the Spearman rank correlation between per-feature open-loop action-chunk divergence (measured on 10k recorded frames) and closed-loop success delta?" If ρ is high (>0.7), then screening features for cloth becomes a batched open-loop problem: you can sweep thousands of features against recorded cloth interaction frames (need a cloth dataset — DROID has some? There's also the possibility of recording a few hours of cloth teleop). Compute after: GPU-parallel open-loop sweeps across all features and many VLAs, closed-loop only for top-k.

B. Change the objective: from uniform-precision success estimation to screening/ranking with early stopping (successive halving / SPRT). Bottleneck: 150 rollouts per feature regardless of effect size; most features likely null. Assumption: that the quantity needed is a precise success estimate per feature rather than a decision (this feature matters / doesn't). Measure: retrospective reanalysis of existing 20,250 episodes — replay the data under successive-halving and count how many episodes are needed to recover the same top features. Cost: no GPU, just analysis. Compute after: each unit of compute buys progressively refined ranking (anytime), and total episodes scale with log of feature count times effect-size, not linear. Fails if: effect sizes are all tiny and near the noise floor so early stopping can't separate — but then the whole approach is dead anyway. Question: "What fraction of the 135 features can be correctly accepted/rejected at α=0.05 with ≤20 rollouts under an SPRT, using the recorded episode outcomes?"

C. Attack the sim-to-real assumption for steering deltas (not absolute performance). Bottleneck: claim that sim batching "pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth)". The assumption smuggles in that *steering effects* inherit the full sim-to-real gap; but the delta from an activation-space intervention might transfer even when the base policy doesn't, because the feature was extracted from real-robot activations (SAE fit on real data?) — actually unclear where activations came from. Hmm, the SAEs are fit on VLA activations — those come from rollouts in some environment. If fit on sim activations, features may be sim-specific. Still, the test is cheap: take features with known real effects, steer in sim, compare deltas. Measure: rank correlation of steering delta sim vs real across ~10-20 features on rigid tasks (data partly exists for real; sim needs building a mirror of the tabletop task — ManiSkill has pi0.5? LIBERO is sim already for pi0.5). Actually COAST on LIBERO-10 is sim; DROID results are real. A mirror: pick a task present both in a real setup and sim. Cost: one engineer-week to set up mirrored sim envs + ~2 GPU-days of batched sim rollouts. If correlation holds, then the 256-GPU-environment RLinf-VLA-style infrastructure becomes directly usable for interpretability sweeps, and compute buys orders-of-magnitude more features/tasks. Fails if: steering deltas don't transfer even on rigid tasks (then sim screening is dead and you must fix cloth sim first).

Also worth considering: changing the unit of work from "SAE feature" to "learned steering direction via direct search" — but conceptors already do something like this; less clean.

Another: order of steps — currently fit SAE first (6,700 Adam steps, GPU-hours), then evaluate features. Interleave: use the evaluation signal to decide what to fit (e.g., fit SAEs only on layers/activations where a cheap causal probe says the layer matters for contact events). Or: fit one SAE jointly across tasks so amortized. The layer-localization reframe: measure which layers' activations predict contact events (probe on recorded data with force/contact labels), then fit SAEs only there. That's also decent. Question: "In which layers do linear probes decode contact events from activations, and does steering there..." Hmm, this is a reasonable third candidate but I think C is stronger because it directly attacks the stated blocker ("false for cloth" — the text flags it as the known wall).

Let me also reconsider: the root question is about cloth/dish-rack tasks. The stated unknown: "whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks." So the deepest reframe: why is answering that question expensive? Because closed-loop cloth evaluation is expensive both in sim (bad physics) and real (slow, sequential). Reframe A addresses it: screen features against recorded cloth data open-loop. But there might be little cloth data in DROID... DROID has some deformable-object episodes? DROID is mostly rigid household tasks; there is some cloth. There exist cloth datasets (e.g., "Cloth funneling"? The "folding" datasets from RT-2 era?). The measure can be: record 2-5 hours of teleoperated cloth episodes (cheap, days), then run the open-loop sweep.

Alternatively reframe the objective: instead of "does a feature control cloth behavior" (existence question — yes/no!), the text's own hint: "Ask whether the objective is the right one: the single best answer, a ranking, a distribution, a rare tail, or a yes or no." The question "does ANY feature control deformable behavior" is a yes/no existence question — cheaper than ranking all features. To answer yes/no you need one positive: search smartly (e.g., gradient-based optimization of a steering direction for a cloth proxy metric) rather than enumerating features. If direct optimization finds a direction that changes cloth behavior, answer is yes regardless of whether it corresponds to a clean SAE feature. That's a nice reframe: change the unit of work from "enumerate SAE dictionary" to "optimize a direction in activation space against a differentiable cloth proxy" — compute then buys search quality (CMA-ES / gradient if proxy differentiable). But the proxy metric for cloth (coverage, fold quality) needs sim, and cloth sim is bad... but coverage of cloth by a gripper path can be measured in real from cameras; expensive closed loop again. Hmm, could use open-loop proxy: maximize divergence toward actions labeled "spreading cloth" in a small labeled dataset. That collapses into A.

I'll go with A (open-loop divergence screening), B (successive halving reanalysis), C (steering-delta sim-real transfer). These map nicely onto "what is measured," "the objective," and "what is held fixed (the belief that sim deltas don't transfer)/order of steps."

Now fill all the schema fields for each:

Fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior.

Note "exact" — probably the exact experiment/protocol. "expected" — expected outcome. "fails_if" — condition under which the reframe is not worth pursuing. "closest_prior" — nearest existing work.

Reframe A (open-loop screening):
- bottleneck: Each feature evaluation waits on 150 sequential closed-loop rollouts (300 steps × 150ms each), so testing whether features control contact-rich behavior costs months of serial robot/sim time; unbatched rollouts idle the GPU.
- assumption: That the only meaningful measurement of "a feature controls behavior X" is closed-loop task success, requiring the causal chain of 300 sequential observations.
- reframe: Change what's measured: replace closed-loop success with open-loop action-divergence — the shift in the VLA's predicted action chunks when a feature is clamped/ablating, computed on recorded contact-rich observations. Recorded frames break the step-to-step dependency: every (frame, feature) pair is independent, so thousands of steered forward passes batch on one GPU.
- question: "Across the existing 135-feature sweep, what is the Spearman rank correlation between open-loop action-chunk divergence (L2/KL on recorded frames) and closed-loop success delta per feature?"
- measure: Re-run each of the 135 steers as a single batched forward pass over ~10k recorded episodes frames from the same tasks; compute divergence vs. unsteered; correlate with the already-measured 150-rollout success deltas. ~1–3 A100-days, zero new rollouts.
- compute_after: If ρ≥~0.7, screening becomes embarrassingly parallel: sweep all 520 SAEs × all features against recorded cloth/dish-rack frames (a few GPU-weeks), reserve closed-loop rollouts for top-k; more GPUs linearly increase features screened per day.
- exact: hmm — "exact" maybe the exact measurement protocol. Let me write: exact protocol: for feature i, Δ_i = mean over frames of ||a_steered − a_base||₂ on the action chunk; rank features by Δ_i; compute Spearman ρ against published success deltas; then prospectively test top-5 open-loop features on one cloth task with 25 rollouts each (125 rollouts, ~2 days on one robot).
- expected: Moderate-to-high rank correlation on rigid tasks (steering that does nothing closed-loop also does nothing open-loop); the open-loop screen discards >80% of features at <1% of the rollout cost.
- fails_if: Open-loop divergence is uncorrelated with closed-loop success (documented risk: open-loop L2 poorly predicts closed-loop success for VLAs) — then the screen is worthless and recorded-frame evaluation can't replace rollouts.
- closest_prior: OpenVLA / π0 evaluations noting open-loop L2 doesn't predict closed-loop success; RLinf-VLA's batched rollouts are the closed-loop alternative (1.61–1.88× with 256 ManiSkill envs); open-loop action-token prediction accuracy used as proxy in VLA training papers.

Reframe B (objective: screening not estimation):
- bottleneck: 20,250 episodes spent as 150 rollouts × 135 features with uniform precision; most features presumably have near-zero effect, so most episodes buy no information.
- assumption: The objective is a precise per-feature success rate (hence 150 trials each), rather than a decision: does this feature matter, yes/no, or which few are worth testing on cloth.
- reframe: Change the objective from estimation to ranking/screening: successive halving / SPRT allocates rollouts adaptively, killing null features after ~10 rollouts and concentrating budget on candidates near the decision boundary; compute becomes an anytime resource that buys discrimination among top arms instead of uniform confidence intervals.
- question: "Using the recorded outcomes of the 20,250 completed episodes, what fraction of features can be accepted/rejected at α=0.05 with ≤20 rollouts under an SPRT, and does successive halving recover the same top-10 features with ≤30% of the episodes?"
- measure: Pure reanalysis: replay episode outcomes in random order under SPRT and successive-halving schedules; count episodes consumed and compare selected set to the full-data ranking. Cost: hours of analyst time, no GPU, no robot.
- compute_after: If the retrospective saving is >3×, every future sweep (including the cloth question) gets the same factor; compute then buys breadth — more SAEs, more VLAs, more tasks — at fixed wall-clock.
- exact: Exact: implement SPRT per feature with H0: success delta = 0 vs H1: |delta| ≥ 0.2 (the observed effects are +9..+21/25, huge), α=β=0.05, on the logged per-episode success sequence; report median episodes-to-decision; run 100 random orderings for stability.
- expected: Given effect sizes of +9 to +21 out of 25 (36–84 percentage points) and the 39/40→0/40 ablation, most decisions are obvious within 10–20 episodes; expect ≥70% episode reduction.
- fails_if: Most features have small true effects near the noise floor (|delta| < 5 percentage points), so early stopping cannot separate them — but that would itself mean steering effects are mostly negligible, a finding in itself. Also fails if episode outcomes aren't i.i.d. (drift over the sweep), inflating SPRT error rates.
- closest_prior: Hyperband/ASHA in hyperparameter search; best-arm identification bandits; SPRT (Wald 1945); LLM-eval adaptive stopping work (e.g., "tinyBenchmarks" / IRT-based efficient evals).

Reframe C (sim-to-real of deltas):
- bottleneck: The stated wall: GPU-parallel sim rollouts "pay only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth)" — so the one proven 1.61–1.88× parallelization route is written off, and all contact-rich evaluation stays serial on real hardware.
- assumption: That steering-induced *deltas* inherit the full sim-to-real gap of the underlying task; i.e., because absolute cloth behavior is wrong in sim, the effect of an activation intervention must also be wrong.
- reframe: Hold fixed the wrong thing differently — test transfer of the delta, not the behavior. SAE features are fit on VLA activations, which encode the model's own (real-data-trained) contact priors; the sim gap may live in the physics, while the feature→action-delta pathway is a property of the network. Measure rank correlation of steering deltas between a mirrored sim task and the real task.
- question: "Across ≥12 features with known real-robot effects on a rigid tabletop task, is the Spearman correlation between sim-measured and real-measured steering success-deltas ≥0.7 — and what is it for one deformable task (towel fold)?"
- measure: Build sim mirrors of 2–3 already-published real steered tasks (setup: days–1 week), run batched sim rollouts (256 envs, RLinf-VLA style) for ~12 features × 100 rollouts = 1,200 sim episodes (~1–2 A100-days), reuse published real numbers for the rigid delta, and run 25-rollout real checks for ~6 features on the towel fold (~150 real episodes, ~2–3 days on one DROID setup). Total ~1–2 weeks.
- compute_after: If rigid-task deltas transfer (ρ≥0.7) and even cloth shows positive correlation, the entire interpretability sweep moves to batched sim: compute buys orders-of-magnitude more features and tasks, and the 420k-rollout scale becomes cheap; real rollouts reserved for final validation of top candidates.
- exact: Exact protocol: pick features spanning the observed real effect range (+9, +15, +21/25 and the 4 general features whose ablation drove 39/40→0/40); replicate each steer in ManiSkill/Isaac mirror of the DROID tabletop setup; delta_i = success(steer_i) − success(base) in each domain; Spearman ρ across features, with bootstrap CI.
- expected: Rigid-task deltas plausibly transfer (the tasks already work in both domains); cloth is the open bet — even ρ≈0.5 on cloth would justify sim pre-screening with real confirmation.
- fails_if: Even rigid-task deltas fail to correlate (ρ<0.3) — meaning the intervention pathway itself is sim-sensitive, so sim screening is dead at any fidelity and the field must either fix cloth physics or pay serial real rollouts forever.
- closest_prior: RLinf-VLA (256 parallel ManiSkill envs, 1.61–1.88×) as infrastructure; sim-to-real gap for deformables documented in cloth-sim work (e.g., Blender/Flex cloth benchmarks); correlation-of-treatment-effect transfer is the analogue of "sim-to-real transfer of policy rankings" studied in RL (e.g., works showing method rankings can transfer even when absolute scores don't).

Also each needs "compute_after" — what more compute buys after the reframe. Done.

Length: keep each field reasonably concise but informative. Return only JSON.

Let me draft the JSON now. Ensure valid JSON, no trailing commas. Keep strings with escaped characters as needed. Avoid special characters issues. Use plain ASCII where possible; avoid ≥ maybe use >=. I'll use plain text like ">=0.7".

Write it fully.

Reframe 1 fields:

bottleneck: "Testing one feature costs 150 sequential closed-loop rollouts (300 steps each, every step waiting on a 150 ms forward pass plus the next observation), so answering whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behavior means months of serial robot or simulator time; an unbatched rollout also leaves the GPU idle while the sim steps."

assumption: "That the effect of a feature can only be measured as closed-loop task success, i.e. the unit of measurement is a 300-step episode in which each observation causally depends on the previous action."

reframe: "Change what is measured: score each feature by its open-loop action-chunk divergence (L2 or KL between steered and unsteered predicted actions) on recorded contact-rich frames. Recorded observations break the step-after-step dependency, so every (frame, feature) pair is independent and thousands of steered forward passes batch on one GPU; closed-loop rollouts are reserved for the handful of features the screen promotes."

question: "On the existing 135-feature rigid-task sweep, what is the Spearman rank correlation between per-feature open-loop action-chunk divergence (measured on ~10k recorded frames) and the already-measured closed-loop success delta per feature?"

measure: "Recompute each of the 135 steers as batched forward passes over ~10k recorded task frames (about 1.35M forward passes, 1-3 A100-days batched, zero new rollouts), rank features by divergence, and correlate against the published 150-rollout success deltas; the episode logs already exist, so this is pure GPU inference plus an afternoon of statistics."

compute_after: "If the screen validates (rho >= 0.7), the cloth question becomes embarrassingly parallel: sweep all 520 SAEs x all features against a few hours of recorded cloth and dish-rack teleoperation in GPU-weeks instead of robot-years, and spend serial closed-loop rollouts only on the top-k; each added GPU buys a linear increase in features screened per day."

exact: "Delta_i = mean over frames of ||a_steer_i - a_base||^2 on the action chunk (plus KL over chunked action tokens as a robustness check); Spearman rho and bootstrap CI between Delta_i and closed-loop delta across the 135 features; prospective confirmation: top-5 open-loop features get 25 real rollouts each on one towel-fold task (125 episodes, ~2 robot-days)."

expected: "High correlation on rigid tasks - features that do nothing closed-loop also perturb nothing open-loop, and the big effects (+9..+21/25, 39/40 to 0/40) should produce large divergences; expect the screen to discard >80% of features at under 1% of the rollout cost."

fails_if: "Open-loop divergence does not rank closed-loop success (rho < ~0.3), which VLA folklore and some evaluations suggest is possible: small per-step action shifts can compound or vanish under closed-loop feedback, in which case recorded-frame screening is worthless and the sequential rollout dependency is real."

closest_prior: "Documented open-loop vs closed-loop gaps for VLAs (open-loop L2 predicting closed-loop success poorly, noted around OpenVLA-class evaluations); RLinf-VLA (1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill envs) is the closed-loop batching alternative this reframe would beat; action-token prediction accuracy is already used as a cheap proxy during VLA training."

Reframe 2:

bottleneck: "The 20,250-episode answer was bought as 135 features x 150 rollouts at uniform precision; if most features are near-null, most episodes purchased no information, and the same waste scales to any cloth sweep."

assumption: "That the objective is a precise success estimate per feature (hence 150 trials for every feature), rather than a decision - is this feature worth testing on cloth, yes or no - or a ranking of the top few."

reframe: "Change the objective from estimation to screening: run a sequential probability ratio test or successive halving over features, killing nulls after ~10 rollouts and concentrating budget near the decision boundary. Compute becomes an anytime resource that buys discrimination among top candidates instead of uniform confidence intervals over all 135."

question: "Replaying the recorded outcomes of the completed 20,250 episodes: what fraction of the 135 features are correctly accepted or rejected at alpha=0.05 within <=20 rollouts under an SPRT, and does successive halving return the same top-10 features using <=30% of the episodes?"

measure: "Retrospective reanalysis only: implement SPRT (H0: delta=0 vs H1: |delta|>=0.2, alpha=beta=0.05) and successive halving on the logged per-episode success sequences, average over ~100 random episode orderings, and compare the selected feature set and episodes consumed to the full-data answer. Cost: hours of analyst time, no GPU, no robot."

compute_after: "If the retrospective saving is >=3x, every future sweep inherits it: the same robot-week screens 3-10x more features, SAEs, or tasks, and the budget freed is what pays for the first contact-rich sweeps on real hardware."

exact: "Per feature, replay episodes in shuffled order; record episodes-to-decision under SPRT and under SH with brackets at 10/30/90 rollouts; report median and 90th-percentile savings, false-accept/false-reject rates vs the full-data labels, and the rank correlation of the SH top-10 with the full-data top-10."

expected: "Large savings: the reported effects are enormous (+9 to +21 out of 25, and 39/40 to 0/40), so most decisions are statistically obvious within 10-20 episodes; expect >=70% episode reduction with identical top-features."

fails_if: "Most true effects are small (|delta| < 5 percentage points) so no early rule can separate them - but that itself would be the finding that steering effects are mostly negligible; also fails if outcomes drift over the sweep (non-i.i.d.), which inflates SPRT error rates and must be checked from the logs."

closest_prior: "Wald's SPRT; Hyperband/ASHA and best-arm-identification bandits in hyperparameter search; adaptive-subsampling work in LLM evaluation (tinyBenchmarks, IRT-based efficient benchmarks) applying the same idea to expensive evals."
